name: India
governanceModel: Non-binding guidelines currently in force; officials have signaled intent to move toward a binding, risk-based AI law
debateTopics: India signals a possible shift toward binding AI legislation
IT Rules 2026 takedown triggers criticised as overbroad by digital-rights groups
Emergency shutdown powers for high-risk AI systems under consideration
overview:
India's approach may be shifting. As recently as November 2025, MeitY's India AI Governance Guidelines were explicitly non-binding and light-touch. On 6 July 2026, MeitY Secretary S. Krishnan signaled that the government intends to prepare a draft AI law that could designate banking, finance, health and critical infrastructure as a high-risk tier, using hedged language ('probably the time has come now to look at a separate legislation'). Reporting around the same date indicates the government is weighing emergency shutdown powers for AI systems in that tier, a notably assertive tool few other jurisdictions have proposed — though as of this writing no draft bill, consultation paper, or timeline has been published, so the precise scope of any such law remains unconfirmed.

What is already binding is narrower: the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules 2026, in force since February 2026, mandate labelling and provenance metadata for synthetic content and a 3-hour takedown window for unlawful AI content (2 hours for non-consensual intimate imagery) — down sharply from a prior 36-hour window. Digital-rights group IFF has reportedly criticised those rules as opaque with overbroad takedown triggers, though this specific attribution has not been independently re-verified against a primary IFF statement.

currentDirection.summary: Officials' public rhetoric has moved from 'no separate AI law needed' toward openness to drafting one within eight months, with a senior MeitY official using hedged language about timing and no draft bill yet published. Reporting indicates the government is also weighing emergency shutdown powers for high-risk AI systems, a notably assertive tool most peer jurisdictions haven't proposed — though the specific scope and design of any such power remain unconfirmed.

recentDevelopments.text: India's private-sector AI-infrastructure build-out accelerates: Reliance announced (February 2026 AGM) a reported ₹10 lakh crore (~$110B) seven-year AI push anchored by a multi-gigawatt, renewable-powered data centre in Jamnagar (first phase targeting 3GW, with an initial ~120MW slated to come online in late 2026), signed its first AI data-centre deal with Meta in June 2026, and is working with NVIDIA on an India-focused foundation model; Adani has announced comparably large plans, together positioning India as a major AI-infrastructure hub.

The IndiaAI Safety Institute, established under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, advances: MeitY approved a further tranche of responsible-AI projects (reported as around 13) targeting deepfakes, bias and evaluation tooling, and issued a call for research partnerships, though the institute's full staffing and independent capacity remain unconfirmed.

policyAndRegulation.title: IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules 2026
policyAndRegulation.summary: Mandatory labelling and provenance metadata for synthetic content; 3-hour takedown window for unlawful AI content on government or court order (2 hours for non-consensual intimate imagery), down from 36 hours previously.

policyAndRegulation.title: India AI Governance Guidelines
policyAndRegulation.summary: Non-binding, light-touch, principle-based guidelines proposing an AI Governance Group, Technology & Policy Expert Committee, and an IndiaAI Safety Institute. Whether these bodies have actually been constituted/staffed since the November 2025 announcement is unconfirmed, and officials have since signaled openness to binding legislation that could eventually supersede parts of this approach.

researchEcosystem.summary: Applied AI research in India includes AI4Bharat (an IIT Madras initiative building Indian-language AI tooling since 2020) and the IndiaAI Mission's subsidised compute portal, which has onboarded more than 38,000 GPUs for startups and researchers under a ₹10,372 crore (~$1.25B) programme. No dedicated AI-focused think tank was identified in this pass, though several general policy institutes plausibly do AI-relevant work.

debates.topic: India signals a possible shift toward binding AI legislation
debates.summary: Within eight months, official rhetoric shifted from 'no separate AI law needed' toward openness to binding legislation with a high-risk sector tier, though no draft bill has yet been published.
debates.expanded: MeitY's November 2025 guidelines were explicitly non-binding. On 6 July 2026, MeitY Secretary S. Krishnan used hedged language ('probably the time has come now to look at a separate legislation') signaling intent to prepare a binding, risk-based AI law — potentially covering banking, finance, health and critical infrastructure as high-risk. One secondary summary states explicitly that no draft bill, consultation paper, or timeline exists yet. If it materializes, this would mark a genuine change in direction, plausibly driven by mounting deepfake incidents and cyber-risk concerns, though it's not yet clear whether this reflects a broader philosophical shift on innovation-friendliness or a narrower, sector-specific response.

debates.topic: IT Rules 2026 takedown triggers criticised as overbroad by digital-rights groups
debates.summary: The sharply shortened takedown windows for AI-generated content have reportedly drawn criticism from at least one digital-rights group (IFF) for opaque, overbroad triggers that could sweep in lawful content, though this specific attribution has not been independently re-verified.
debates.expanded: Reporting attributes to the Internet Freedom Foundation, and possibly other digital-rights groups, the argument that the rules' takedown triggers lack clear definitions and due-process safeguards, risking over-removal of legitimate content. The government has defended the shortened windows (down from 36 hours to 2-3 hours) as necessary given the speed at which deepfakes and non-consensual imagery spread. The precise wording and attribution of the IFF criticism have not been independently confirmed against a primary IFF statement.

debates.topic: Emergency shutdown powers for high-risk AI systems
debates.summary: India is reportedly weighing emergency shutdown powers over AI systems in high-risk sectors — a notably assertive regulatory tool few other jurisdictions have proposed, though the precise scope and design remain unconfirmed.
debates.expanded: If adopted, emergency shutdown powers would let authorities forcibly halt AI systems operating in banking, finance, health or critical infrastructure in the event of serious malfunction or harm. A 6 July 2026 official source indicates the government is 'weighing' such powers, corroborated by secondary reporting, but no draft bill or consultation paper exists yet, so the specific scope, sectors covered, and legal design remain unconfirmed. Should it proceed as described, this would go further than most peer jurisdictions' AI laws, which generally rely on fines and compliance orders rather than direct operational shutdown authority.
